title: Reconstruction of human cognitive circuits after neurons have been lost

concept.text: This innovation would restore cognitive function by replacing neurons lost from an adult human brain and integrating the replacements into functioning circuits. The goal is to recover a computation impaired by neuronal death—for example, the ability to learn new information—and the everyday abilities that depend on it. Producing neurons or keeping a graft alive would be intermediate achievements; success would require the replacement cells to contribute to the recovered cognitive capacity. This is the target defined by the supplied materials, not a capability they demonstrate.

Conceptual synthesis: replacement must supply appropriate neuronal classes and connect them to an already organized brain. Depending on the damage, this could require rebuilding local cortical or hippocampal circuitry and reconnecting it with surviving networks. Amyloid clearance, dopamine replacement, axon repair and increased plasticity may support treatment or repair, but none alone establishes that replacement neurons have reconstructed a lost cognitive circuit.

significance.text: Conditional significance: if replacement neurons restored cognitive computations lost through neuronal death, the direct consequence would be recovery of the capacities those computations support. Sustained gains in new learning and independent daily function would represent a different therapeutic outcome from merely slowing further deterioration. Successful reconstruction could therefore change the prospects of people whose disability reflects neuronal loss, although its applicability would depend on the location and extent of damage and the condition of surviving circuitry.

Restoring the machinery of memory does not automatically restore the information once stored in it. Specific autobiographical memories could return only if enough relevant information survived elsewhere or could be independently reconstructed. Replacement neurons might enable new learning without recovering a person's lost life events. This distinction limits claims that circuit reconstruction would reverse every consequence of neurodegeneration or restore a prior mental state in full.

Conditional downstream possibilities include rehabilitation that uses restored learning capacity and repeated repair during a chronic disease. These possibilities would additionally require control of continuing pathology, durable integration and an acceptable treatment burden. The salamander-like regeneration analogy in the research notes can illustrate the ambition of replacing damaged tissue, but it does not establish that human cognitive circuitry or lost memory content can regenerate in the same way. The supplied evidence does not support a historical attribution for that analogy, and feasibility and timing remain highly uncertain.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central research challenge is to make appropriate replacement neurons restore a cognitive computation within an adult human brain after neuronal loss. The supplied animal report provides relevant evidence of tissue growth and nervous-system integration, but it does not establish this human outcome. Conversely, the limited evidence collection cannot establish that the target is absent from every part of the field as of 1 November 2026.

Engineering synthesis: concrete barriers include generating the required neuronal identities, delivering them to the appropriate sites, supporting survival and maturation, and establishing suitable incoming and outgoing connections. A replacement cell must participate in the relevant pattern of activity, rather than simply show neuronal markers or form some synapses. Repair may require coordinated reconstruction across several cell classes and regions; a surviving graft in one location would not by itself establish that this coordination has been achieved.

Scientific synthesis: an adult brain presents a different integration problem from tissue growing into an available space in an animal model. Researchers would need to determine how replacement cells acquire useful connections within surviving networks and how those networks learn to use them. In progressive neurodegeneration, repair must also remain effective despite the disease environment. Practical barriers include controlling excessive or inappropriate growth, maladaptive activity, immune responses and damage from delivery. These are proposed engineering concerns, not findings established by the retained source excerpt.

A further unresolved capability is convincing measurement of functional reconstruction. Structural evidence can identify cells and connections, but cognitive improvement could arise from effects on surviving neurons or other treatment mechanisms. Establishing the breakthrough therefore requires converging evidence that replacement neurons are functionally integrated and contribute to the recovered capacity, with causal tests where feasible and appropriate.

current_state.text: The reviewed portion of Max Kozlov's Nature news article, dated 16 September 2026, reports that transplanted human brain tissue can grow into much of the vacant space in mice lacking a key brain region and wire into their nervous systems. The caption identifies the absent region as cerebral cortex. This supports animal tissue-occupancy and integration groundwork. It does not establish restoration of cognition after adult human neuronal loss.

Access to that Nature article was partial: access options replaced most of the article in the retained copy, even though the extraction was not marked as truncated. The available material does not establish host age, how the cortex became absent, detailed experimental methods or cognitive restoration outcomes. The earlier description of neonatal mice filling a cortex that never developed therefore exceeds what the reviewed material supports. The news article lists a September 2026 Kaganovsky and colleagues paper with DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-11032-2, but its full text was not supplied for review.

The research notes also describe a 2022 study by Revah, Gore, Kelley and colleagues in Nature 610, 319–326, DOI 10.1038/s41586-022-05277-w. They report that human cortical organoid grafts integrated in developing rodent hosts and could influence reward-seeking behavior. No retained source artifact or source URL for that study was supplied for this review, so these details remain an attributed research-note summary. If confirmed, such behavioral participation would be relevant groundwork, while still leaving adult human cognitive reconstruction unestablished.

For lecanemab, the research notes identify van Dyck, Swanson, Aisen and colleagues, New England Journal of Medicine 388, 9–21 (2023), and report mean worsening on the Clinical Dementia Rating–Sum of Boxes at 18 months of 1.21 points with lecanemab and 1.66 with placebo. They also report amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema in 12.6%. Taken as reported, those results describe less decline while both groups worsened, rather than reversal of impairment. However, the source index contains no retained NEJM text, so the review could not independently verify the numbers, endpoint interpretation or adverse-event context. The missing artifact is an evidence limitation, not evidence that these reported results are false. Amyloid-treatment outcomes alone would not demonstrate reconstruction by replacement neurons.

The research notes describe a Brain review dated 3 September 2025 as covering a 12-person, uncontrolled phase 1 bemdaneprocel dopamine-cell trial. They attribute a modest response in the high-dose group and no significant accompanying change on 18F-DOPA PET imaging to that review. No retained Brain artifact was supplied, and the notes record difficulty reloading the page for full author confirmation. The trial design, clinical finding and PET statement therefore remain unverified here. As described, this is early, motor-focused dopamine-replacement work; even a confirmed motor benefit would not establish reconstruction of cortical or hippocampal cognitive circuits.

The supplied bounded-search record is empty, so the collection cannot support a comprehensive statement about the field as of 1 November 2026. Its dated reports remain relevant within their respective evidence limits. The reviewed material demonstrates neither achievement of the full human target nor its definitive absence across all current research.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: in people with documented neuronal loss from a neurodegenerative condition, an intervention produces sustained improvement in a prespecified cognitive capacity, such as new learning, together with improved independent daily function. The result should exceed merely slowing decline. A preregistered controlled design should address practice effects, changes in supportive care, symptomatic stimulation and other plausible explanations. These are proposed criteria for a convincing demonstration, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained cognitive recovery and improved independent function exceed slowing decline

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanistic evidence: validated imaging, tissue evidence where available, or other appropriate measurements identify replacement neurons of the relevant lost classes. Functional measurements should show useful synaptic integration, and converging evidence should link the replacement cells to the recovered capacity. Cell survival, anatomical connections or cognitive improvement alone would each leave important alternative explanations unresolved. Causal perturbation could strengthen the inference where ethically and technically feasible.
completion_criteria.label: Replacement neurons integrate synaptically and contribute to recovered cognition

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: demonstrate the effect across independent cohorts and, where feasible, independent centers; define the disease, severity, anatomical damage and patient characteristics for which it works; and follow durability, continuing neuronal loss, adverse growth, maladaptive activity and treatment burden. Follow-up duration and clinically meaningful improvement thresholds should be specified and justified for the application. Finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, not universal repair of every cognitive circuit or neurodegenerative disease.
completion_criteria.label: Replicate effects across independent cohorts and report practical boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Recovery of particular autobiographical memories should be an additional outcome only where their information remains available or can be independently reconstructed. It should not be mandatory for demonstrating restored new-learning capacity. A Parkinson's motor-score improvement alone would not meet this cognitive-circuit criterion, and animal graft integration would remain an intermediate demonstration requiring further translation.
completion_criteria.label: Stronger: Recover autobiographical memories using available or reconstructable information

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: NEU-04, Content-faithful reading and writing of specific episodic memories, concerns the information carried by memories. NEU-06 concerns rebuilding the neuronal machinery that supports cognition. The two could overlap if reconstructing a circuit also required restoring specific memory content, but successful neuronal replacement need not recover lost autobiography, and writing a memory need not replace dead neurons.

Roster-based comparison: NEU-05, Target-specific regrowth of long axons in the adult mammalian central nervous system, could help replacement neurons reach the correct distant targets. Its central challenge can also arise in surviving neurons with damaged axons, without neuronal replacement. NEU-11, Reversible, circuit-specific reopening of critical-period plasticity in the adult brain, could help surviving and replacement cells reorganize their connections; increasing plasticity alone does not supply missing neurons. These entries retain distinct objectives despite their potential contribution to NEU-06.

Roster-based comparison: NEU-08, A generative developmental code that builds a specified functional neural circuit, overlaps the challenge of producing an organized replacement circuit. Its title does not require repair inside a damaged adult human brain. NEU-09, Cell-type-specific molecular access throughout the intact adult human brain, could support targeting, monitoring or control of relevant cells, but access alone would not reconstruct a lost computation.

Roster-based comparison: NEU-01's simultaneous spike-resolved recording, NEU-02's whole-brain synaptic connectomics and NEU-03's predictive theory of circuit computation could help measure, design or explain reconstruction. NEU-07's noninvasive cellular-resolution reading and writing could support assessment or control. These are potentially enabling capabilities with distinct endpoints; NEU-06 does not require that each be fully achieved before a bounded repair demonstration could succeed.

Roster-based comparison: NEU-10, A causal, measurement-grade account of conscious content, and NEU-12, An account of sleep sufficient to complete its necessary functions without a normal sleep period, address different explanatory and functional targets. Cognitive-circuit reconstruction could interact with conscious experience or sleep-dependent function, but the supplied titles provide no basis for treating either as equivalent to neuronal replacement. These comparisons use the supplied roster titles; detailed specifications for the other entries were not supplied.

change_log.change: Preserved NEU-06's identity while distinguishing its target capability from a field-wide assertion that it remains unavailable.
change_log.reason: The partial evidence and empty freshness record cannot establish comprehensive availability or absence as of the stated cutoff.

change_log.change: Retained the lecanemab numerical outcomes and dopamine-graft details as explicitly attributed, unverified research-note reports.
change_log.reason: This preserves useful quantitative detail without treating candidate quotations as independently reviewed evidence or treating missing artifacts as disproof.

change_log.change: Narrowed the 2026 mouse-graft account to tissue occupancy and nervous-system integration, and removed definitive neonatal and developmental interpretations.
change_log.reason: The retained Nature excerpt does not establish host age, the origin of cortical absence or cognitive restoration.

change_log.change: Preserved the 2022 organoid study summary with its missing-artifact limitation.
change_log.reason: It supplies relevant integration and behavioral context, but its reported findings were not verified in the supplied review.

change_log.change: Replaced obligatory biographical-memory recovery with a prespecified cognitive-capacity outcome and treated specific memory recovery as conditional.
change_log.reason: Replacing neurons does not itself recreate information destroyed with the original circuit.

change_log.change: Added functional contribution, causal corroboration where feasible, reproducibility and practical boundaries to the proposed completion criteria.
change_log.reason: Structural markers alone cannot establish that replacement neurons caused cognitive recovery.

change_log.change: Expanded concrete engineering barriers and conditional downstream implications as labeled synthesis.
change_log.reason: The record needs to explain what reconstruction entails without presenting inferred challenges or future possibilities as demonstrated findings.

change_log.change: Compared related concepts using the supplied roster and retained the regeneration analogy without historical attribution.
change_log.reason: Roster titles permit bounded comparisons; neither full neighboring specifications nor evidence for the historical attribution was supplied.

unresolved_issues: The lecanemab endpoint values, both-group worsening interpretation and 12.6% edema figure need verification against retained primary-source text and their clinical context.
The bemdaneprocel trial size, control design, clinical response and reported absence of significant 18F-DOPA PET change remain unverified in this evidence package.
The 2022 organoid study's host conditions, integration measurements and behavioral results require its underlying source for verification.
The full 2026 Kaganovsky paper is needed to establish host age, model construction, experimental scope and functional outcomes; the partial news excerpt cannot resolve these details.
No bounded freshness search establishes the full state of adult human cognitive-circuit reconstruction as of 1 November 2026.
Clinically meaningful cognitive and daily-function thresholds, follow-up duration and feasible causal measurements remain application-specific proposals.
Detailed boundaries with neighboring concepts remain provisional because only their roster titles were supplied.

The review's recommendation to omit unverified clinical details from the factual account was adapted by retaining them as clearly attributed reports, because the requested consolidation calls for preserving useful quantitative detail with explicit uncertainty.
